Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-29
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (NimbleDocs PM), Samir Khan (NimbleDocs Eng Mgr), Liu Wei (NimbleDocs ML Eng)

Auto-generated sections (may be imperfect):
Summary: quick hosted API chat/text generation walkthrough; streaming explained; param demos for temp, top_p, stop tokens; retry/backoff patterns; console inspector demo; discussion about latency target (sub-300ms median) and cost controls.
Topics: see metadata list.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Ava from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account. Diego is our SE, he'll do the walkthrough. How's everybody doing?
[00:00:08] Priya Patel: good, thanks. we have about 40 minutes. main goal is to see how hosted API would behave for our in-editor assistance flow. latency and cost kinda the big ones.
[00:00:18] Diego Morales: great, thanks Priya. quick agenda: 1) live API demo with streaming, 2) tweak generation params, 3) discuss retries/backoff and fallback model strategies, 4) console quick-look and optimize suggestions. sound ok?
[00:00:29] Samir Khan: yep, that works. we usually aim for <300ms avg for token generation in our editor, sometimes a bit spiky.
[00:00:36] Liu Wei: and we have a budget target per 1k requests, so want to see token cost implications.
[00:00:41] Diego Morales: perfect, i'll start with a short curl streaming example and then the JS SDK so you can see chunking in the client.
[00:00:47] (screen share starts)
[00:00:52] Diego Morales: ok, here's a simple request to the generations/chat endpoint. note we set "stream": true so responses come as partial deltas. the client will receive multiple data frames, each roughly corresponds to new tokens or token groups.
[00:01:06] [Speaker 1]: (inaudible) so the important bit is the client can start rendering before finalization, right?
[00:01:12] Diego Morales: yes exactly. for interactive editors that's the big win — perceived latency drops because you show partial answers while the model continues. the SDK handles parsing the stream frames, we have examples for node/python.
[00:01:24] Priya Patel: how do you handle stop sequences and partial sentences? we don't want mid-sentence truncation.
[00:01:29] Diego Morales: good question. stop sequences are honored on finalization, but the stream can still emit tokens up to the stop. we recommend using explicit stop tokens and also setting a conservative max_tokens cap. and on the client side, you can buffer until you see stop or an end event. worth noting the streaming deltas can be re-ordered in rare network conditions, so the SDK gives you sequence ids to assemble reliably.
[00:01:49] Samir Khan: sequence ids? we didn't see that documented elsewhere.
[00:01:52] Diego Morales: yeah, in our streaming frames we include a partial index — sometimes the transcriber labels differ but it's in the payload. in the console inspector you can see those fields live.
[00:02:00] Priya Patel: what's the typical packet size? do we get single-token frames or grouped?
[00:02:05] Diego Morales: both. small models yield smaller frames; larger ones batch tokens to be efficient. you can configure a tradeoff via the runtime param 'stream_chunk_size' (internal name may vary in docs) though the default is optimized. grouping reduces overhead but increases per-frame latency a bit.
[00:02:18] Liu Wei: let's talk parameters: temperature, top_p, max_tokens — show us an example of the effect.
[00:02:23] Diego Morales: sure. i'll run three side-by-side calls: temp 0.0 deterministic, temp 0.7 balanced, temp 1.2 creative.
[00:02:29] [00:02:29] Diego Morales: (runs requests)
[00:02:34] Diego Morales: you can see low temp reduces variability; with temp 0.0 we often recommend beam/greedy which cuts token waste — good for cost and predictability. higher temp yields more diverse completions but also more token usage chasing longer branches.
[00:02:48] Priya Patel: is there a good rule of thumb for top_p vs temperature?
[00:02:52] Diego Morales: top_p controls nucleus sampling. if you set top_p 0.9 and temp 0.7 you get moderate diversity. the simplest pilot is run with temp 0.2-0.5 and top_p 0.8 and tune. also limit max_tokens aggressively for short snippets.
[00:03:04] Samir Khan: cost-wise, do you charge per input + output tokens?
[00:03:08] Ava Chen: yes per-token pricing on hosted API. embeddings are separate. we provide a token estimator in the console and also token-level cost breakdowns per request in logs so you can see which prompts are expensive.
[00:03:18] Priya Patel: about retries — if a request times out or we get 503s, what's the recommended pattern?
[00:03:22] Diego Morales: recommended is exponential backoff with jitter, and short retry window for interactive flows. e.g., try once with 150-300ms jitter, then 2nd attempt at ~700ms if needed; after 2-3 retries switch to a fallback model (lower-cost, lower-latency) or a cached response. we also support automatic fallback routing in the routing policy if capacity is constrained.
[00:03:45] Liu Wei: where do you store cached prefixes? we need to ensure privacy.
[00:03:48] Diego Morales: prefix/KV caching happens at the request layer; for hosted we keep optional ephemeral cache — you can opt out. for Dedicated/Private you control networking and can disable server-side caching and use customer-managed KMS.
[00:03:59] Priya Patel: security: do you support SSO and SOC2?
[00:04:03] Ava Chen: yes — SOC 2 Type II, SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integrations. i'll attach the security pack after the call.
[00:04:11] (short pause)
[00:04:15] Diego Morales: switching to console — this is the request inspector, here you can replay a request, view token breakdown, latency per stage (queue, compile, model execution). you can also annotate sample prompts and pin a model version for rollouts.
[00:04:31] [Speaker 2]: the UI looks snappy.
[00:04:34] Diego Morales: thanks — for pilots we recommend pinning a small model variant for most traffic and routing a % to a higher-quality model for A/B. that reduces cost while you evaluate quality.
[00:04:44] Samir Khan: do you have SDK-level retry helpers or do we implement ourselves?
[00:04:48] Diego Morales: the JS SDK includes a small retry helper with exponential backoff and jitter; we show examples in the docs. for streaming, if a connection dies mid-stream, the SDK can resume from the last committed token by using the KV cache / prefix id which reduces re-computation. (note: resume behavior has caveats with certain model variants).
[00:05:07] Priya Patel: interesting — can we test resume in the pilot?
[00:05:09] Ava Chen: absolutely. Diego can include resume scripts in the benchmark package.
[00:05:14] Diego Morales: switching to a low-latency demo: i'll run a short 1-token-per-step loop to show per-token latency.
[00:05:20] (typing sounds)
[00:05:26] Diego Morales: ok here the median per-token is ~85ms from a us-west region to our hosted endpoint under current test conditions. your mileage will vary depending on client geography + network.
[00:05:35] Liu Wei: 85ms sounds ok; our 300ms target might be achievable with edge regions. do you support region pinning?
[00:05:40] Ava Chen: yes we have region routing; you can fix traffic to a region for latency. for strict regulatory workloads, Dedicated or Private is recommended.
[00:05:47] Priya Patel: about quality monitoring — can we track regressions if we change params or models?
[00:05:51] Diego Morales: yes Redwood Optimize hooks into your eval sets; you can run evals on rollout and set alerts when metrics degrade. we also keep per-prompt diffs so you see which prompts regressed.
[00:06:02] Samir Khan: any gotchas with streaming + retries? like duplicate tokens on retry?
[00:06:07] Diego Morales: duplicate tokens are possible if you re-request from scratch. best practice: use prefix ids, commit the last stable token index, then resume; the SDK does a small reconciliation step to avoid duplication. if you do naive retries you may get repeated content.
[00:06:20] Priya Patel: what about rate limits? we have bursts with hundreds of users typing.
[00:06:24] Ava Chen: hosted API has rate limits per account and route; for bursty traffic we recommend Dedicated for predictable throughput or use token bucket smoothing in the client. we can also set up burst capacity overrides for pilots.
[00:06:36] Liu Wei: can you show an example of a retry backoff header or code sample?
[00:06:40] Diego Morales: sure. here's a snippet: exponential backoff base 100ms, multiply by 2 each retry, add 50-250ms jitter, cap at 2 seconds. for streaming, attempt a single short reconnect, then fallback to a non-streaming generation if needed.
[00:06:55] (Diego pastes code in chat)
[00:06:58] Priya Patel: for the pilot metrics, we want P50 and P95 token latency, token cost per completion, and failover rate. is that something Redwood telemetry can export?
[00:07:06] Ava Chen: yes — console exports and you can pipe telemetry to your SIEM or use the API for metrics. we'll include a sample dashboard.
[00:07:13] Samir Khan: our legal/security team will ask about data retention and deletion.
[00:07:16] Ava Chen: hosted keeps logs for X by default — i'll attach retention settings; we have options for shorter retention or log redaction, and with Dedicated/Private you can enforce deletion and keep keys client-side.
[00:07:27] Priya Patel: ok, sounds good. any performance tuning suggestions before pilot?
[00:07:31] Diego Morales: yes — 1) conservative max_tokens, 2) reuse conversation history via prefix caching (don't resend entire long context each time), 3) use token batching for server-side requests where multiple completions can be merged, 4) pin lower-latency model for majority traffic and route a small % to high-quality models. Optimize will generate these suggestions automatically for typical workloads.
[00:07:52] Liu Wei: about prefix caching — is that safe for PII? we might have user data in context.
[00:07:56] Diego Morales: you can opt out or encrypt cache keys with your KMS. we'll document recommended redaction patterns.
[00:08:04] (brief pause)
[00:08:07] Diego Morales: any deeper questions? we can do a follow-up deep dive with your infra folks to run benchmarks and simulate spikes.
[00:08:14] Priya Patel: yes please — schedule a 2-hour bench next week with Liu and Samir.
[00:08:19] Samir Khan: also send pricing tiers for hosted vs dedicated and rough break-even points.
[00:08:23] Ava Chen: will do. Diego — i'll loop in solutions for pricing math.
[00:08:27] Diego Morales: i'll prepare the benchmark checklist and scripts; including resume/reconnect tests, streaming latency, and cost per prompt.
[00:08:34] Priya Patel: can you also include a short video of the console inspector so our PM can share with execs?
[00:08:38] Ava Chen: yes, i'll record a 3-minute console walkthrough.
[00:08:42] (wrap-up)
[00:08:45] Ava Chen: recap: we'll send pilot scope + pricing and security docs; Diego sends benchmark assets; schedule 2-hour bench next week. thanks everyone.
[00:08:55] Priya Patel: thanks, useful demo. bye.
[00:08:58] Samir Khan: bye.
[00:09:00] (call ends)
